title.en: The Grave of Makunaima's Brother and the Great Spirit's House
title.zh: 馬庫納伊瑪弟之墓與大神之屋

region.zh: 蓋亞那科廷加河毛伊濟河源

texts.period: Wai-Wai/Akawai tradition recorded by Brown; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XI 'Spirits of the Mountain', §175

summary.en: On a low hill above the Waiquah River, a branch of the Cotinga, Barrington Brown observed a huge artificial mound of earth and small stones which the guide said was the grave of Makunaima's brother. The Great Spirit is a dweller in this region, for an isolated rocky mountain seen from the Cotinga at the head of the Mauitzie River is called Makunaima-outa — 'the Great Spirit's House'.
summary.zh: 科廷加河支流瓦伊夸河上小丘，有巨塚，土石堆成；嚮導言：此馬庫納伊瑪弟之墓也。大神亦居此域：毛伊濟河源孤峰，名曰馬庫納伊瑪奧塔——『大神之屋』。

sensitivity.note: Guiana highland tradition recorded by Brown, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: On a low hill above the Waiquah River, a branch of the Cotinga, Barrington Brown observed a huge artificial mound of earth and small stones, which the guide said was the grave of Makunaima's brother. It would seem that the Great Spirit is a dweller in this region, for an isolated rocky mountain, seen from the Cotinga lower down at the head of the Mauitzie River, is called Makunaima-outa, which means 'the Great Spirit's House'.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §175 (from Brown); not verbatim.

title.en: Roraima Guarded by the Enormous Camudi

region.en: Mount Roraima and Merume escarpment, Pakaraima range
region.zh: 帕卡賴馬山脈羅賴馬山與梅魯梅崖

texts.period: Makusi/Arekuna tradition recorded by Boddam-Whetham; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XI 'Spirits of the Mountain', §175

summary.en: According to the tale told by a medicine-man, Mount Roraima was guarded by an enormous camudi (bush-master snake) which could entwine a hundred people in its folds; he himself had once approached its den and had seen demons running about as numerous as quails. At the Merume escarpment on the upper Mazaruni the Indians begged Brown's men not to roast salt fish on the embers, fearing to rouse the ire of a large eagle and camoodie snake living on the mountain side, who would show their displeasure by causing more rain to fall; another Indian refused to camp near what he believed to be the cave of a celebrated water-mama, near which it was dangerous to sleep.
summary.zh: 薩滿言：羅賴馬山有巨蛇守之，可纏百人；其人曾近蛇穴，見群魔奔走如鶉。馬扎魯尼上游梅魯梅崖，土人誡勿烤鹹魚，恐觸山中之鷹與蛇之怒，令雨更多；又有人不肯宿於水母之穴旁，言其處睡眠危險。

sensitivity.note: Guiana highland traditions recorded by travelers, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: According to the tale told by a medicine-man, Mount Roraima was guarded by an enormous camudi, which could entwine a hundred people in its folds. He himself had once approached its den and had seen demons running about as numerous as quails. At the Merume escarpment, upper Mazaruni, the Indians begged Brown's men not to roast salt fish on the embers, fearing thereby to rouse the ire of a large eagle and camoodie snake, which they said lived on the mountain side, and would show their displeasure by causing more rain to fall.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §175 (from Boddam-Whetham); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another Indian in the same neighborhood objected to camping near what he believed to be the cave of a celebrated 'water-mama', near which it was dangerous to sleep. In the Pakaraima Mountains there is a singular rock called by the Makusis Toupanaghoe, from its resemblance to a hand: the Indians make it the seat of a demon and pass it under fear and trembling.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §175 (from Boddam-Whetham); not verbatim.

title.en: Rocks That Must Not Be Pointed At

region.zh: 蓋亞那埃斯塞基博河

texts.period: Guiana oral tradition; recorded 19th c., summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XI 'Spirits of the Mountain', §176

summary.en: Many a local feature of Guianese scenery constitutes the landmark of some notable occurrence, until the spot becomes weird and eerie. The Old Man's Rock in the Essequibo is haunted by a murdered buckeen, and it is dangerous to point the finger at it. A large bare rock, the Negro Cap, standing near the Three Brothers Islands in the same river, carries a most curious superstition: if any individual points at this rock, a heavy storm will immediately overtake him for his audacity. And in very dry seasons the rocks in the river beds show a curious glazed, black appearance — but any allusion to their appearance would vex these rocks and cause them to send misfortune.
summary.zh: 圭亞那山川多為故事之地而顯靈異。埃斯塞基博河『老人石』為被害土人所祟，指之則凶。三兄弟島旁之『黑奴帽』巨石尤可畏：指之者立遭暴雨以罰其傲。旱季河底諸石黑亮如釉——然言其狀必觸石怒而致災。

sensitivity.note: Guiana oral tradition summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Many a local feature of natural scenery in the Guianas constitutes the landmark of some notable occurrence — a death, a bloody feud, the appearance of some extraordinary animal — with the result that such a spot becomes weird and eerie, and all kinds of fanciful stories are told in connection with its immediate neighborhood. The Indians have a tradition that the cliffs and hillocks about a mile from Kayiwa on the Corentyne are inhabited by a large snake, which from time to time goes to drink the water of the river, and that its passage thither has deprived the cliffs of vegetation.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§175-176; not verbatim.

passages.text: We have the Old Man's Rock in the Essequibo, which a murdered buckeen continually haunts, and at which it is dangerous to point the finger. There is also a large bare rock — the Negro Cap — standing with its head about six feet above the water, close to the Three Brothers Islands in the same river, concerning which the natives entertain a most curious superstition: they believe that if any individual points at this rock a heavy storm will immediately overtake him for his audacity. In very dry seasons, when the water in the rivers is low, the rocks in their beds are seen to have a curious glazed, vitrified and black appearance; but any allusion to their appearance would vex these rocks and cause them to send misfortune.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §176 (citing im Thurn); not verbatim.

title.en: The Water Folk and the Broken Friendship

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍沼地瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §177

summary.en: The Warraus distinguished their water spirits: the Ahüba, 'Fish-mamma', chief of all the fish, with a head like a person's and a body like a fish furnished with all the feet of land animals, who work evil and eat the shipwrecked; and the Ho-aränni and Xaba-ranni, the Water People of sea and river. There was a time when these Water People lived in amity and friendship with the Land People, exchanging wives between the tribes. The Warrau supply ran short, the Spirits became vexed; and the Warraus insisted on isolating their women at menstrual periods — a practice the Water People were unaccustomed to and strongly objected to. So the friendship broke, and the Water People were made bad.
summary.zh: 瓦勞人分水鬼為三：阿希巴『魚母』，魚類之長，首如人、身如魚而具獸足，作惡而食溺者；霍阿蘭尼與沙巴蘭尼則海河之水人。昔水人與陸人相友，互易其妻。後瓦勞婦寡，水人怒；又瓦勞始禁女子經期見人，水人不慣而深惡之。誼遂絕，水人化為惡。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Warraus made several distinctions in their Spirits: they had their Ahüba, Ho-aränni, and Xaba-ranni. The Ahüba is the 'Fish-mamma', the chief of all the fish — one male and one female. The two live in underground water; their heads are like those of people, but their bodies resemble those of fish though they are provided with all the different kinds of feet belonging to land animals. They work evil on mankind; when shipwreck takes place they eat the bodies. The Ho-aränni and Xaba-ranni represent the Water Spirits of the sea and the rivers respectively; they are sometimes like people, sometimes like fish.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §177; not verbatim.

passages.text: Indeed, there was a time when these Water People used to live in amity and friendship with the Land People. The Warraus used to exchange wives with them in those days, a wife being taken as required alternately from the one and the other tribe. The Warrau supply ran short, however, and the Water Spirits accordingly became vexed and angered with them. The second alleged reason is that the Warraus insisted on the isolation of the women at their menstrual periods, a practice to which the Water Spirits were unaccustomed and strongly objected. So the ideal state of existence was terminated, and the Water People were made bad.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §177; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bouto of Ega and the Mother of the Waters

region.zh: 亞馬遜下游埃加鎮

texts.period: Amazonian folk tradition recorded by Bates; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §177

summary.en: The natives of the Amazons country have their mai d'agoa — Mother or Spirit of the Water — in the shape of a water serpent said to be many score fathoms in length, a monster doubtless suggested by the anaconda. One of the mysterious tales told of the Bouto, the great dolphin of the Amazons, was that a Bouto once had the habit of assuming the shape of a beautiful woman, with hair hanging loose to her heels, and walking ashore at night in the streets of Ega to entice the young men down to the water. If anyone was so much smitten as to follow her to the water-side, she grasped her victim round the waist and plunged beneath the waves with a triumphant cry.
summary.zh: 亞馬遜土人有『水母』之說：水蛇長數十尋，蓋由大蟒而想見者也。布托乃亞馬遜巨豚，傳說其一曾化為美婦，長髮委地，夜行埃加街衢，誘青年至水邊；若有痴郎隨之，則攔腰抱之，歡呼而沒於波底。

sensitivity.note: Lower Amazon folk tradition recorded by Bates, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The natives of the Amazons country have their mai d'agoa — Mother or Spirit of the Water — in the shape of a water serpent said to be many score fathoms in length, a monster doubtless suggested by the occasional appearance of the anaconda, which assumes a great variety of forms.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §177 (from Bates); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of the many mysterious tales told of the Bouto, as the large dolphin of the Amazons is called, was to the effect that a Bouto once had the habit of assuming the shape of a beautiful woman, with hair hanging loose to her heels, and walking ashore at night in the streets of Ega to entice the young men down to the water. If anyone was so much smitten as to follow her to the water-side, she grasped her victim round the waist and plunged beneath the waves with a triumphant cry.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §177 (from Bates); not verbatim.

title.en: The Omar of the Falls and the Peaiman's Fire

region.zh: 蓋亞那埃斯塞基博河歐魯波卡里灘

texts.period: Akawai tradition recorded by im Thurn; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §182

summary.en: The Omars are beings with bodies like those of exaggerated crabs and fish, who live under water in the rapids and often drag down the boats of the Indians as they shoot the falls. One at Ouropocari fall used to feed on rotten wood and dragged down many boats merely in mistake for floating logs — but the Indians were drowned all the same. So one day an Ackawoi peaiman carefully wrapped up two pieces of fire-rubbing wood so no water could damp them, dived into the middle of the falls, and got into the belly of the Omar. There he found whole stores of rotten wood, and set fire to them; the Omar, in great pain, rose to the surface, belched out the peaiman and died.
summary.zh: 奧瑪者，似蟹似魚之怪，居灘下水，屢曳沉土人之舟。歐魯波卡里灘有一奧瑪，食朽木，誤舟為浮木而屢沉之，人皆溺死。一日阿卡瓦醫師裹火木二片以防其濕，潛入灘心入其腹中；見朽木成堆，縱火焚之。奧瑪痛極浮出，嘔出醫師而斃。

sensitivity.note: Akawai tradition recorded by im Thurn, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Omars are beings with bodies variously described as like those of exaggerated crabs and fish, who live under water in the rapids, and often drag down the boats of the Indians as they shoot the falls. This Omar used to feed on rotten wood, and he dragged down many boats merely in mistake for floating logs, but all the same the Indians were drowned.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §182 (from im Thurn); not verbatim.

passages.text: So one day an Ackawoi peaiman carefully wrapped up two pieces of the wood with which fire is rubbed, so that no water could make them damp. Then he dived down into the middle of the falls, and got into the belly of the Omar. There he found whole stores of rotten wood. So he set fire to this. Then the Omar, in great pain, rose to the surface, belched out the peaiman and died.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §182 (from im Thurn); not verbatim.

title.en: The Piai in the Water Spirit's Belly

region.zh: 蓋亞那莫魯卡河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §182A

summary.en: Fishermen kept disappearing down the river, caught by a Ho-aränni. The piai's son went to investigate and was swallowed too. The piai then traveled with benab posts, firewood and fire aboard his corial; turning a point, boat and all were engulfed in the Water Spirit's open jaws. In the darkness he lit his fire and set up his benab, sticking half a dozen rods deep into the spirit's belly. Ho-aränni consulted three medicine-men in vain — 'It is all your own fault and you must die' — and rose gasping to the surface like a poisoned fish. On the third gasp the piai saw the trees, shoved himself and his corial out of the creature's jaws, and hastened home: 'I am come only to show myself, for with all the heat my hair is dropping off and I must die.' And he did die soon. Fortunately our ancestors killed most of the bad Water Spirits, which is why they are so scarce now.
summary.zh: 漁者屢失蹤，皆霍阿蘭尼所吞。醫師之子往察亦被吞。醫師乃載棚柱柴火而行；至灣，舟與人皆入鬼口。黑暗中生火立棚，柱深深釘入鬼腹。霍阿蘭尼遍求三醫無效——『皆爾自取，必死』——遂如中毒之魚浮出喘息。醫師伺其三喘，見林木，乃推舟出其顎而歸。曰：『吾惟現身一見，熱甚，髮落將死矣。』果卒。幸先祖多誅惡水鬼，故今稀矣。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Plenty of men would go fishing down the river, but every now and again one of their number would disappear: a Ho-aränni, one of the Water Spirits, caught him. The son of the local piai traveled to the spot where the 'accident' always took place, and was himself caught and taken away. It was now the turn of the piai to say, 'I will go to the place where my son disappeared'; wise in his generation, he carried with him, in his corial, benab posts, firewood, and fire. Turning a point, his boat was suddenly engulfed within the open jaws of the Water Spirit lying there in wait: boat, posts, firewood, and fire were all swallowed with him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §182A; not verbatim.

passages.text: When at last the piai came to his senses he was in complete darkness; so after lighting his fire he made himself comfortable and set up his benab, sticking half a dozen rods in regular sequence deep into the Water Spirit's belly. Ho-aränni experienced acute pain and consulted a piai friend, who could give him no relief; a second said: 'It is just what you can expect for treating people of my profession in the way you do'; and the third, of even greater renown: 'There is nothing to cure you. It is all your own fault and you must die.' The pains becoming so strong, the Water Spirit rose out of the water just as a fish does when poisoned with the haiari root, rising to the surface and gasping for breath.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §182A; not verbatim.

passages.text: The piai inside kept a sharp lookout: on the first gasp he recognized an immense sheet of water — they were still far out at sea; on the second, a small bush in the far distance; on the third, clearly the trees. Taking the next opportunity of the spirit rising to the surface, he shoved himself and his corial out of the creature's jaws and hastened home. 'I am come only to show myself, for what with all the heat my hair is dropping off and I must die.' And he did die soon. Several of the Water Spirits used to be bad like this one, but fortunately for us present Warraus, our ancestors killed most of them, and this is the reason they are so scarce now.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §182A; not verbatim.

title.en: Sisters Porpoise and Sea-cow

region.zh: 蓋亞那莫魯卡河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §183

summary.en: Two sisters had a bush-cow (tapir) for a sweetheart; every day they gathered plums in the field, made drink from them, and whistled for him with their fingers to their mouths. Their brother suspected, followed, and mimicking their whistle shot the tapir and cut the body to pieces. Next day the girls whistled and whistled, but no lover came; finding the mangled remains, they cried, determined on throwing themselves into the water — and did so: one sister turned into a manati, the other into a porpoise.
summary.zh: 二姊妹以貘為情郎；日日採李釀酒，以指入口作哨喚之。兄疑而窺之，效其哨聲引貘出而射殺之，碎其屍。翌日姊妹呼之不至；尋見殘骸，相泣，共投於水：一化海牛，一化海豚。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Once there were two sisters who had a Bush-cow [tapir] for a sweetheart: he used to live with both of them. They had a habit of regularly going to their field, collecting the plums, of which their lover was so fond, and making drink from them; when it was ready they whistled for him to come, by putting their fingers into their mouths and blowing. Their brother in the meantime had his suspicions as to what was going on, so one day he followed them, and without being himself seen watched everything that took place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §183; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon afterward the two girls went to another field to dig cassava. The brother seized the opportunity of visiting the place where the Maipuri lived, whistled as the girls used to do, and as soon as the creature put in an appearance shot him with his arrow, then cut the body into pieces and scattered them. Next morning the girls went as before to the old place to make the plum-drink, and when it was ready they whistled — but no Maipuri came. Tired of whistling, they searched and soon came upon the mangled remains. They both began to cry and determined upon throwing themselves into the water; this they did — one sister turned into a manati, and the other into a porpoise.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §183; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fisherman's Water-jug and Potato

region.zh: 蓋亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §184

summary.en: A fisherman whose catch was invariably large tugged up something on his line that proved to be Oriyu herself, her beautiful hair entangled in it. He carried her home and made her his wife, on the single condition that her origin should never be divulged. She could see fish in the depths no one else could, and the household prospered — until the old mother-in-law, in liquor, let out the secret. Grieved, Oriyu waited her chance; when the crabs began to march from the ocean, the family made up a party, and she told her companions she and her husband would visit her people below and send up something to eat and drink. Up came a large jar of cassiri and a lot of potatoes; and when the jug and skins were thrown back, she turned them into the giant low-low and the squatty little imiri — which is why the low-low is the fisherman's water-jug and the imiri his potato.
summary.zh: 漁者得線所曳，乃水靈奧里尤，美髮纏於釣線。攜歸為妻，誓不洩其來歷。其察水底魚群，無不獲；家道日興。老嫗醉而洩其秘。奧里尤默然，俟機而行：蟹羣上陸之日，全家出遊，忽言將攜夫訪其水下之族，饋食與飲。巨壺卡西里酒與薯自水中湧出；壺與皮擲還，遂化為巨低低魚與矮伊米里魚——故低低乃漁人之壺，伊米里乃其薯。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There was once a fisherman who went fishing daily, and whose catch was invariably large. One day something pulled at his line; once more he tried. Something tugged at the hook; he hauled in the line, and what should he drag up to the surface but Oriyu herself — the real Spirit of the Water, with all her beautiful hair entangled in the line. So beautiful was she that he carried her home to his mother and made her his wife, the only condition Oriyu stipulated being that neither her prospective husband nor her mother-in-law should ever divulge her origin.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §184; not verbatim.

passages.text: Being accustomed to the water, Oriyu proved an excellent helpmate: out she would go with her husband and look into the depths for fish, seeing them when no one else could, advising him not to throw his line in here but over there — and so day after day they returned home with plenty of fish for the old mother-in-law. This happiness came to an end when the old woman, in liquor, loosened her tongue and let out the secret of Oriyu's origin. Oriyu said nothing, so grieved was she, but waited her opportunity to take her husband with her to her former home under the waters.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §184; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the next occasion that the crabs began to 'march' from out the ocean to the shore, the family made up a large party in a big corial. Oriyu told her companions that she and her husband were about to pay a visit to her people below, but would not be gone long, and would send up something to eat and drink — they must share everything fairly. Without more ado she and her man dived into the water. After a while up came a large jar of cassiri and a lot of potatoes. When they had eaten and drunk their fill they threw the jug and the useless skins back into the water, where the Oriyu turned the former into the giant low-low and the latter into the squatty little imiri. This is why we old Arawaks always speak of the low-low as the fisherman's water-jug, and of the imiri as his potatoes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §184; not verbatim.

title.en: Arawanili and the First Rattle: Oriyu's Gift
title.zh: 阿拉瓦尼利與首鈴：水靈之賜

region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克島

texts.period: Arawak tradition recorded by Brett; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §185

summary.en: Out on one of the islands all the men, women and children were struck down with sickness. Arawanili, the island chieftain, begged Oriyu for a charm to withstand the Evil Spirit's power which had made his people sick. She gave him the branch of an ite tree, told him to plant it and bring back the first fruit that fell — a calabash. Having emptied the rind through holes cut in it, she provided the feathered handle, dived into the sea, and brought back shining white stones to put into it; with these she showed him how to invoke the spirits. Thus was the first maraka (rattle) formed; and besides this she taught Arawanili the use of tobacco, till then unknown to man.
summary.zh: 島中疫起，老幼皆病。酋長阿拉瓦尼利求水靈奧里尤賜符以抗邪鬼之力。彼賜伊提棕之枝，令植之，取初落之果——葫蘆也。穿孔空其殼，裝以羽柄，自海底攜白石納其中；示以召鬼之法。首鈴於是成。又授菸草之法，世人未知者也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak tradition from Brett 1880, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Out on one of the islands all the men, women, and children were struck down with sickness at the same time, and there was no charm among them strong enough to withstand it. Arawanili, the island chieftain, begged Oriyu for some charm to withstand the Evil Spirit power which had made his people sick, and the Water Spirit heard his prayer.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §185 (from Brett); not verbatim.

passages.text: She gave him the branch of an ite tree, which she told him to go and plant, and to bring back to her the first fruit that should fall from it. This turned out to be a calabash, with which he did what he was told. Having emptied the rind through certain holes cut in it, she provided him with the feathered handle, and dived into the sea whence she brought the shining white stones to put into it; with these she thereupon showed him how to invoke the Spirits. Thus was the first maraka (rattle) formed. Besides this, she taught Arawanili the use of tobacco, till then unknown to man.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §185 (from Brett); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Water Spirit Got the Man's Wife from Him

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §187

summary.en: A man left his wife at a benab on an island while he fished; about midnight the Water Spirit visited her, told her of his great love, and told her to blame her husband entirely for leaving her alone. Next morning she refused to share her husband's hearth any more, and stepping from the boat where the water came to her knees, walked away with the Water Spirit along the river-bank. The husband fetched her mother with the silver nose-ornament and bead bracelets and necklets the wife had left; the spirit vanished as they came near, and the daughter murmured: 'Your son-in-law caused this trouble: he would not let me come into the corial with him.' 'You will see me sometimes, but never distinctly: directly you think you see me clearly, I will disappear.' No one knew then that the Water Spirit had taken advantage of the man also — it was this spirit who had made him refuse to let his wife come with him.
summary.zh: 夫留婦於中流棚而自捕魚；夜半水鬼至，言其深愛，且令歸咎於夫。翌日婦絕夫而去，自舟中下水，與鬼並行岸上。夫攜其母及銀鼻飾珠鐲往見；鬼忽隱形。婦曰：『汝婿致此禍：不許我同舟。』『汝偶或見我，然必不分明；汝以為看真切時，我即隱去。』當時無人知水鬼亦欺其夫——正此鬼令其不許婦同舟也。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man took his wife with him on a fishing expedition, built a benab on an island in midstream, and told his wife to remain there while he went to fish. She was very anxious to accompany him in the corial, but he insisted on her remaining. Being very tired, she fell asleep, and about midnight the Water Spirit paid her a visit. He told her who he was, of his great love for her, and that he would now take her to wife: all she had to do was to tell her previous husband that it was entirely his fault that she had been left alone, and that henceforth she declined to share his hearth and home.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §187; not verbatim.

passages.text: So when he returned next morning from his fishing the wife made a clean breast of everything, blaming him because he had refused to let her accompany him in the corial, and told him further that she intended living with him no more. 'After today you will not see me. You must tell all my family to meet me tomorrow at a spot that I will show you.' As they traveled she showed him the spot, the boat stopped as if held, and she got out, the water coming up to her knees, while the corial continued on its journey. The husband looked back and saw his wife with another man, the Water Spirit, stepping ashore.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §187; not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother especially was angry, but was mollified when he assured her that next day he would take her to the place where her daughter had left him, and gave her a message to bring the silver nose-ornament and the bead bracelets and necklets. Coming close, the Spirit suddenly disappeared. The mother handed over the beads and ornaments, while her daughter murmured: 'Your son-in-law caused this trouble: he would not let me come into the corial with him.' Mother and daughter sobbed, and the daughter said: 'You will see me sometimes, but never distinctly: directly you think you see me clearly, I will disappear.' No one knew at the time that the Water Spirit had taken advantage of the man also: it was this Spirit who had made the husband refuse to let his wife keep him company in the corial.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §187; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Water Woman Secured a Landsman for Husband

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §187A

summary.en: A corialful of men paddled down to catch crabs; one heard a voice behind him: 'Brother! I am come. My father sent me to you to give me a quake of crabs.' He handed them over and paid with the loan of his body. She told him the boat would suddenly stop of itself on the way home — he must jump into the water and join her, and she would bring him to his own home later. Exactly so it happened: he jumped out at the stopping-place, and his friends left him standing in the water where the girl held him up. Her father sent him home for the crab-feast on one condition — if any disturbance or fighting at the sport, he must come back at once. That evening his wife and in-laws threatened to beat him for sporting with the strange girl; he rushed back to the landing where two Water Women were waiting, and the old Ho-aränni father said, 'Take my two daughters to wife.'
summary.zh: 一舟人下海捕蟹；忽聞身後聲曰：『兄！我至矣。父命來取一筐之蟹。』與之，以身相酬。婦言舟行必自停一處，屆時躍水相會，後當送其還家。果然；眾棄之於水。其父縱之歸家赴蟹宴，惟約曰：席間有爭鬥則速返。夜其妻與內親以私通外女之故欲毆之；遂奔登處，二水女在焉。老霍阿蘭尼父曰：『以吾二女妻汝。』

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A corialful of men were paddling down the river to catch crabs. They reached the sea, and while hunting among the bushes one of the party heard a noise behind him, and turning around was much surprised to see a young woman there, and still more so when he heard her say: 'Brother! I am come. My father sent me to you to give me a quake of crabs.' Having handed them over to her, she paid him with the loan of her body. Before departing she told him that, while the boat containing him and his friends would be passing up the creek on the way home, it would suddenly stop of itself in a certain spot: he was then to jump into the water and join her, and she would bring him to his own home later on.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §187A; not verbatim.

passages.text: This is exactly what did occur. After a while the corial suddenly came to a standstill, our friend jumped out, and his friends left him standing in the water where the girl was holding him up. In the meantime the erring spouse was taken by the Ho-aränni girl to her people below, and her father told him he had been sent for because his daughter wanted him. 'You can go home to your own people this very day, and enjoy the feast of crabs. I make only this one condition: if there is any disturbance or fighting at the sport, you must come back here at once. I am sending both my daughters with you.' The two girls took him to his own landing-place, telling him to shut his eyes; when he opened them he found himself on land close to his house.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §187A; not verbatim.

passages.text: But as the evening progressed the people began to be quarrelsome in their cups, with the result that his brothers-in-law, sisters-in-law, and wife all threatened to beat him for sporting with the strange girl. He rushed out of the place right back to the landing, where the two Water Women were awaiting him. When he told them how his people had commenced to interfere and threatened to beat him, they took him back into the water, where the old Ho-aränni father said: 'Take my two daughters to wife.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §187A; not verbatim.

title.en: The Moon-sick Girl and the Water Spirit (Carib)
title.zh: 經期少女與水鬼（加勒比）

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §188

summary.en: A young girl had reached the age when she was developing certain signs indicative of approaching womanhood. Her mother went as usual to work in the field, but on her return was much surprised to see neither daughter nor house — in place of the latter a large sheet of water. She said Okoyumo must have carried her girl away and began to weep. When her husband came back from the chase she told him the Water Spirit had swallowed her daughter; 'I do not want to live without my girl,' he cried, 'Okoyumo must swallow me also,' and so saying, jumped into the flood. The Spirit of the Water, however, did not want to punish him and would not let him drown, but just made him float level with the surface — he could not be sick in the same way as the girl. It is the scent of a woman's sickness when in that condition that makes her so attractive to Okoyumo.
summary.zh: 少女將成人；母田作歸，但見水汪汪一片，屋與女皆失。言必奧庫尤莫攜女去，泣。夫獵歸聞之，呼曰：『無女不能活，奧庫尤莫亦當吞我！』遂躍洪流。水鬼不欲罰之，不使溺，浮其身與水面平——蓋其無經期之穢也。惟婦人彼時之氣味，最為水鬼所嗜。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A young girl had reached the age when she was developing certain signs indicative of approaching womanhood. Her mother went as usual to work in the field, but on her return was much surprised to see neither daughter nor house, and in place of the latter a large sheet of water. She said that Okoyumo must have carried her girl away, and began to weep.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §188; not verbatim.

passages.text: When her husband later on came back from the chase, she told him that Okoyumo had swallowed her daughter, and this news upset him much. 'I do not want to live without my girl,' he cried; 'Okoyumo must swallow me also,' and so saying, he jumped into the flood. The Spirit of the Water, however, did not want to punish him, and so would not let him drown, but just made him float level with the surface; he of course could not be sick in the same way as the girl. It is the scent of a woman's sickness when in that condition that makes her so attractive to Okoyumo.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §188; not verbatim.

title.en: The Moon-sick Girl and the Water Spirit (Warrau)

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦卡波阿溪

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §189

summary.en: A little girl caught a little fish entirely different from anything she had ever seen — so pretty, with beautiful eyes, a slim body covered with red spots — and kept it in a watered hole by the house, where the water never dried up. When it had grown big she freed it at her bathing place, and as soon as she got into the water it would nestle close to her. Her mother warned her it was not a real fish but the Ho-aränni himself, and never to go near the stream when moon-sick. Her advice was not heeded: on the fourth touch the Water Spirit swallowed her. Her piai father dived into the underground cavern, and before Ho-aränni killed him he blew his shell; his relatives dug quickly, unearthed the pair, killed the Water Spirit, and left his bones to rot on Wakapoa Creek. Why was the piai killed? Because he ought not to have gone alone.
summary.zh: 幼女得一奇魚：目美身纖而紅斑遍體；畜於家側水穴，水不涸。長而放之於浴處；女入水，魚輒依偎其側。母誡曰：『此非魚，乃水鬼也；汝經期毋近水。』女不聽，第四觸之，遂被吞。為醫之父潛入鬼之地下穴，臨死吹螺；親屬聞聲疾掘，出其屍，誅水鬼，棄其骨於瓦卡波阿溪而朽焉。醫師何以死？以獨行也。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There was once a little girl by the river-side catching fish with a cassava-sifter. She caught one little fish entirely different from anything she had ever seen; it was so pretty, with beautiful eyes, and a slim body covered with red spots. 'What a pretty fish you are!' she exclaimed; 'I must really keep you all for myself.' So she put it alive in water in her calabash and took it home, where she dug a little hole near the house, poured water into it, and placed the fish there — and strange to say the water never dried up. The fish gradually grew bigger and bigger, and when it had arrived at a good size its guardian, who had already entered womanhood, took it down to the water-side just where she used to bathe, and set it free.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §189; not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as she got into the water it would approach and nestle quite close to her. The mother often saw it swimming about there, and would warn her daughter that it was not a real fish but something else — and when it got very big she recognized it as the Ho-aränni, the Water Spirit. Then she warned her girl especially to keep out of the stream when she was moon-sick; but her advice was not heeded, and the young woman insisted next day on bathing. On the fourth touch the Water Spirit swallowed her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §189; not verbatim.

passages.text: The father was sorely grieved and asked the Ho-aränni why he had treated his daughter in that shameful manner, but the Water Spirit defended himself by saying she had insisted on bathing too soon after she had been moon-sick, and that he had already warned her three times. Being a piai, the father knew where to find the Water Spirit; collecting his relatives, he told them that when they heard him blow his shell they must dig at the spot indicated. He dived into the underground cavern of the Water Spirit, and there Ho-aränni killed him — but before he died he blew his shell; his friends heard him, dug quickly, unearthed the pair, killed the Water Spirit, and left his bones to rot on Wakapoa Creek. Why was the piai killed? Because he ought not to have gone alone; when people start on such expeditions they should always have company.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §189; not verbatim.

title.en: How Sickness and Death Came to the Warraus from the Water People

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §190

summary.en: A fisherman wished for a wife from among the Ho-arännis; one appeared waist-high above the water and clambered into his corial. Her father below welcomed him on a live alligator bench — which is why the Warraus carve their benches in that likeness — and sent back a message: he must send his sister for the spirit's son. But the wife's one command was that at her moon-sickness she must stay in the hut, not be sent to the naibo-manoko: 'if I die, my father will have a spite against you, and send you sickness and death.' The Warrau women insisted on custom; she was found dead there the following morning. 'From now on sickness, accident, and death will come among your people from mine, and if any of your women-folk travel on water while moon-sick, my people will draw their shadows.' Before that time Warraus never had accidents or death; they had only moon-sickness. Later, forgetting the warning, he and his friends set out to sea in two big canoes; the Water People shot them down with round-knobbed arrows and unchained their sharks — for these people keep sharks as we keep dogs — which tore the drowned bodies to pieces. Thus the Water People punished the Warraus.
summary.zh: 漁者願娶水族之女；一女半身出水，登其舟。其父以活鱷為凳延客——瓦勞雕凳作鱷形由此始。妻誡曰：『吾經期毋送我出戶；若致死，吾父必遷怒於汝，降病與死。』族婦執舊俗送之出；翌晨已死。鬼父曰：『自今病、厄、死皆自我族入汝族；汝族婦人經期行水者，我必抽其影。』昔瓦勞無厄無死，惟有經期。後其人忘誡，與友泛海；水人以圓頭箭射沉二舟，縱鯊——彼等畜鯊如吾儕畜犬——碎溺者之屍。水人罰瓦勞如此。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man went fishing, and wished for a wife from among the Water People, the Ho-arännis. One day, while fishing, one put in an appearance waist-high above the surface and came quite close. 'Would you like to take me home with you?' was the first question she asked him; when he told her 'Yes', she clambered into his corial, and he took her home. She told him not to roast the morokot fish he had caught but to boil it, and impressed him that for the future he must never bring fish for her to eat, but only animals and birds.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §190; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day she went with him in the corial, got into the water, and came up with a message from her father: he would be glad to welcome him below. The man was afraid, but she stood straight up in the water, which came to the level of her hips — 'Come along! Don't be frightened' — and he jumped in close by her side. She bent down, seized the head of a big water-camudi, clamped its jaws on the gunwale, and led the way below. He found himself in the house of his father-in-law, who gave him a bench to sit on which was really a large live alligator — this is how it has come to pass that we Warraus always use a bench carved in the likeness of that creature.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §190; not verbatim.

passages.text: His wife warned him: when she was moon-sick he must not send her away to the naibo-manoko, but let her remain in the hut; if she died there, her father would send sickness and death. The Warrau women insisted on custom; she was found dead in the out-house the following morning. When the widower threw himself into the water and reached her father's house, the old man said: 'Why didn't you listen to my daughter? From now on sickness, accident, and death will come among your people from mine, and if any of your women-folk travel on water while they are moon-sick, my people will draw their shadows.' Before that time Warraus never had accidents or death. By and by, forgetting the warning, he and his friends started to sea in two big canoes: the Water People shot at them with round-knobbed arrows, both boats sank, and the Water People unchained their sharks — for these people keep sharks as we keep dogs — which tore the bodies of the drowned to pieces. Thus the Water People punished the Warraus.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §190; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bore on the River: Mother of Waters

region.zh: 蓋亞那伯比斯河怒潮

texts.period: Arawak/Carib coastal tradition; recorded 19th-20th c., summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §191

summary.en: The tidal wave, or bore, known as appapuru on the Berbice and other streams, is ascribed to the bad things of the deep: when the river becomes inconveniently low for them, they show their uneasiness by moving furiously about and thus agitate the river. The tribes on the coast usually give it some name signifying 'head of waters' or 'mother of waters', and in connection with this have many strange stories to tell of the Loku-kuyuha (people's spirit) mermaid, or 'watery mamma'. Wailak-paru, a creek on the right bank of the Potaro, is believed to be the home of Oriyu: the turbulence of the water as it runs into the Potaro is caused by water issuing from the body of that Spirit.
summary.zh: 伯比斯諸河之怒潮，土名阿帕普魯，皆歸於水中惡物：水淺不便其居，則狂動而撼河。濱海諸族名之曰『水首』『水母』，並有水靈洛庫庫雅（人鬼）人魚之異聞。波塔羅右岸之瓦伊拉克帕魯溪，相傳為奧里尤之居；其水入波塔羅之洶湧，即彼身中流出之水也。

sensitivity.note: Coastal Guiana tradition summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The tidal wave, or bore, known as appapuru on the Berbice and other streams, in certain of this colony's rivers is a case in point. Among the natives the popular explanation is that when this River becomes inconveniently low for the bad things of the deep, they show their uneasiness by moving furiously about, and thus agitate the river. The several tribes on the coast usually give it some name signifying 'head of waters' or 'mother of waters', and in connection with this have many strange stories to tell of the Loku-kuyuha (people's spirit) mermaid, or 'watery mamma' as they translate it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §191; not verbatim.

passages.text: Wailak-paru, a creek on the right bank of the Potaro, is so called from a part of the human body, and is believed to be the home of Oriyu: the turbulence of the water as it runs into the Potaro is caused by water issuing from the body of that Spirit.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §191; not verbatim.

title.en: Amanna and Her Talkative Husband

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §192

summary.en: Heated with the fumes and liquor of a big paiwarri feast, an Indian went to the pond to cool himself and was met by Amanna, one of the Okoyumo nation, who invited him into the water. Below the surface he saw houses, plenty of people, and many young women, and was offered drink; but Amanna took him straight to her old father, who welcomed him and instructed his daughter to look after him properly. His mother, tracing his tracks to the water's edge where they disappeared, mourned him a long time as dead. He visited her, went back to his water wife, visited again — and each time his little brother asked point blank whether he was living with the Okoyumo People. The third time, drunk, the brother pressed; 'Yes, I am!' replied the exasperated man, 'and this is my wife, Amanna, one of that nation.' Directly she heard this she made all haste to the waterside and jumped in, her husband in close pursuit; and as soon as he got below, her friends and relatives set on him and killed him for having mentioned her name and told people who she was.
summary.zh: 宴罷酒酣，一印第安人就池沐浴；遇奧庫尤莫族女阿瑪納，邀入水中。水下屋宇人群皆備；女引見其老父，父善遇之。其母循跡至水涯而絕，久以為溺死。夫三歸省；幼弟屢直問：『兄居奧庫尤莫族乎？』第三次弟醉而逼問；夫怒答：『然！此吾妻阿瑪納，其族之女也。』女聞言疾奔水邊躍入，夫追之；甫入水，其親族群起殺之——以其言其名、告人以其所自也。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Heated with the fumes and liquor of a big paiwarri feast, an Indian succeeded in making his way to the pond where he intended bathing his skin and getting cool. On arrival there he was met by Amanna, one of the Okoyumo Nation, a very pleasant-spoken woman, who asked him to join her in the water. He demurred at first, but what with her repeated requests coupled with the attractiveness of her charms he ultimately consented, promised to be looked after, and went below: he saw a number of houses, plenty of people, and many young women, and felt quite content. Amanna would have none of the drink offered, and took him straight away to her old father, who gave him welcome and instructed his daughter to look after him properly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §192; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the meantime the man's mother had missed him from the convivial gathering and, following his tracks to the water's edge where they disappeared, mourned him a long time as dead. When at last he visited her he gave 'a walk-about' as his excuse, and on his second return found his mother and little brother drinking paiwarri; the latter questioned him point blank as to whether he was living with the Okoyumo People. 'How dare you ask me such a question?' — and back to the water he hurried, remaining longer than before. Amanna had in the meanwhile borne him three children; leaving them behind, he told his wife to accompany him on a visit to his mother.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §192; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the drinking party the little brother was absolutely drunk, and nothing would do but he must ask his elder brother as before whether he was living with the Okoyumo People. 'Yes, I am!' replied the exasperated man, 'and this is my wife, Amanna, one of that nation.' Directly the woman heard this she made all haste to the waterside and jumped into the water, her husband in close pursuit. As soon as he got below, her friends and relatives set on him and killed him for having mentioned her name and telling people who she was.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §192; not verbatim.

title.en: Forbidden Words on the Water

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍-莫魯卡河阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §194

summary.en: The surest way of offending the Water Spirits — and thereby getting caught in a storm, capsized, wrecked, or drowned — is to utter certain words strictly forbidden on a boat. Among the Arawaks of the Pomeroon and Moruca Rivers certain terms must never be employed but paraphrased: the gun becomes 'the foot', the dog 'the one with the teeth', the fowl 'load on the head', the horse 'round foot', the cow 'horn', the tiger 'the frothing one', the medicine-man 'the one with wisdom'. The Warraus had various words strictly taboo when traveling by boat; in Cayenne it is dangerous to name the streams and islands passed, even the medicine-men, on pain of rain, shipwreck, and some frightful monster rising from the deep to swallow the whole lot.
summary.zh: 冒犯水鬼最速之法，莫如舟中出禁語——立招風暴、翻覆、溺斃之罰。波默龍-莫魯卡之阿拉瓦克人行舟必諱言而易之：槍曰『足』，犬曰『有齒者』，雞曰『頂載』，馬曰『圓足』，牛曰『有角』，虎曰『沫吼者』，醫師曰『有智者』。瓦勞亦有舟中禁語；卡宴土人並忌呼所過川島之名，犯者降雨、覆舟，或有怪物自深淵出而盡吞之。

sensitivity.note: Arawak/Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The surest way of offending the Water Spirits, and thereby getting caught in a storm, and being capsized, wrecked, or drowned by way of punishment, is to utter certain words strictly forbidden under the circumstances. Thus, among the Arawaks of the Pomeroon and Moruca Rivers, there are certain terms which must never be employed when on a boat: they have to be paraphrased. The occupants of a corial will never be heard to use the term arcabuza (gun), but speak of a gun as kataroro (foot, referring to the stock); they talk of kariro (the one with the teeth) instead of perro (dog); of kanakara-shiro (load on the head, the cock's comb) instead of gallina (fowl); of akwadoa-kotiro (round foot) instead of caballo (horse); of kakwaro (horn) instead of vaca (cow); of chedoa (frothing, in reference to its snarling) instead of aroa (tiger); of katau-chi (the one with wisdom) instead of the medicine-man.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §194; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Warraus also had various words strictly taboo when traveling by boat. The same holds good for Cayenne, where the superstitious Indians take care not to speak of several things by their right names: a rock must be described as 'that which is hard', a lizard as 'that which has a long tail'. It is dangerous also to name the streams and little islands passed en route; even the medicine-men may not be mentioned as such — infringement of this rule will cause at least rain to fall, besides exposing one to shipwreck and to the likelihood of some frightful monster rising from out the deep and swallowing the whole lot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §194; not verbatim.

title.en: Okohi's Last Journey: the Origin of the Sun's Warmth
title.zh: 奧科希末程：日光之暖所自

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §197

summary.en: At the water-side Waiamari's uncle's young wife tried to seduce him; he shouted 'Bilili! Kwahoro!' — 'Incest! Shame!' — and went to stay with his elder uncle Okohi, whose name among the Warraus means the hottest part of the day, the warmth of the sun. Accused and fought, the nephew was taken by Okohi on a long journey in a canoe painted with the sign of the Sun on the bows and a man and moon at the stern, across a big sea, to the house of Assawako, where the youth brought armadillo flesh and played the kahabassa beautifully. When uncle and nephew got back to their own country, old Okohi bathed, seated himself in his hammock, gathered all his family around and spoke: 'When I was young, I could stand traveling day after day, as I have just done; but I am old now, and this is my last journey.' So saying, his head burst, and out of it there came the Sun's warmth and heat.
summary.zh: 瓦伊阿馬里之嬸於水邊誘之；彼呼『亂倫！可恥！』而投長叔奧科希——其名即一日最熱之時，日之暖也。叔姪受誣而鬥；奧科希攜姪遠行，舟首畫日、尾畫人月，越大海至阿薩瓦科之舍，獵犰狳、奏卡哈巴薩之笛。既歸，老人沐浴坐吊床，聚家人而言：『昔我能日日行如今日；今老矣，此吾末程也。』言畢，頭裂，日光之暖與熱自中而出。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Waiamari was the name of a young fellow staying at the house of his uncle. One day he went down to the water-side to bathe; hearing a splash behind him he saw his uncle's young wife chasing him in the water. She whispered 'Don't you want me?' — but instead of replying quietly Waiamari loudly upbraided her by shouting 'Bilili! Kwahoro!' (Incest! Shame!), and the girl drew back. The couple got out of the water; the boy passed on to stay with his elder uncle, Okohi, at whose place he slept that night — for okohi among the Warraus means the hottest part of the day, referring to the warmth and heat of the sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §197; not verbatim.

passages.text: The aunt's husband reproached his nephew for attempted improper conduct and fought him twice, being thrown down each time, until Okohi interfered: 'Boy! That will do.' To save further strife he took Waiamari away with him on his journey, and the youngster painted the sign of the Sun on the bows of the waija canoe, and at the stern a man and a moon — as the Indians' canoes were decorated even up to recent times. They crossed a big sea, the paddle-blades sweeping so that the water sang 'Wau-u! Wau-u!', and landed at the house of the pretty Assawako, where the youth shot a quakeful of armadillo flesh and played the kahabassa so beautifully it sang 'Waru-huru-tia'.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §197; not verbatim.

passages.text: When at last uncle and nephew got back to their own country, old Okohi bathed his skin, and after seating himself in his hammock gathered all his family around and spoke to them as follows: 'When I was young, I could stand traveling day after day, as I have just done, but I am old now, and this is my last journey.' So saying, his head burst, and out of it there came the Sun's warmth and heat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §197; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Moon Got His Dirty Face

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河阿拉瓦克-瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §198

summary.en: Long ago a brother and his sister were living by themselves. Every night after dark someone used to come and fondle and caress the sister — attentions she was far from averse to, but very curious to identify. She therefore blackened her hands with the soot from the bottom of the pepper-pot (the Warraus say with humatímba, the blue paint of the Caribs), and when her lover came that evening smeared her hands over his face. When day dawned she learned it was her own brother who had taken advantage of her. She abused him roundly and told the neighbors, who spread the story far and wide, till everybody shunned him. He is now the Moon, and the marks still recognizable on his face are those his sister imprinted with the soot years ago. Even to this day women do not trust him.
summary.zh: 昔兄妹獨居；每夜有人撫其妹，妹樂之而欲知其人。乃以椒釜底之煙墨手（瓦勞言加勒比人之藍 paint），夜抹其面。天明乃知亂之者即己兄。大罵而告鄰里，事播四方，眾皆棄之。彼今即月也，面上可辨之斑，即昔妹以煙所印者也。至今婦人不信之。

sensitivity.note: Arawak/Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically. Twin/incest-parallel to sky-body origin stories in other traditions.

passages.text: Long ago a brother and his sister were living by themselves. Every night after dark some one used to come and fondle and caress the sister, attentions which she was very far from being averse to, but she was very curious to discover who her unseen visitor was. She could never find out. She therefore blackened her hands one day with the soot from the bottom of the pepper-pot, and when her lover came that evening, she smeared her hands over his face.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §198; not verbatim.

passages.text: When day dawned she thus came to learn that it was her own brother who had taken advantage of her. She was extremely angry, abused him roundly, and told the neighbors, who in turn spread the story of his conduct far and wide. The result was that everybody shunned him, and he became at last so thoroughly ashamed of himself that he declared he would keep away from everyone and live by himself. He is now the Moon, and the marks which can still be recognized on his face are those which his sister imprinted with the soot years ago. Even to this day women do not trust him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §198; not verbatim.

title.en: The Legend of Bat Mountain

region.zh: 蓋亞那帕卡賴馬山脈穆拉帕山

texts.period: Makusi tradition recorded by Schomburgk; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §203A

summary.en: A long, long while ago an immense Bat lived on Murapa-yeng — Bat Mountain — and spread fear and terror among the Makusis. As soon as the sun had sunk in the west the huge creature swept down upon the happy homes and carried off anyone found out of doors to be devoured; not a night passed without an abduction, and the tribe's entire annihilation seemed at hand. The medicine-man exorcised it in vain. To prevent the total destruction of her tribe an old woman arose and declared herself ready to sacrifice herself: stationing herself at night in the middle of the village with a covered fire-stick, she was seized by the creature's frightful claws and carried aloft — where she uncovered the fire-stick, and like the Sun throwing its rays backward (the Comet), the streak of light showed the people the direction of the creature's nest. Next morning the high flames from the burning nest upon the very mountain showed where to go; they succeeded in killing it, and even now immense heaps of bleached bones are to be found there.
summary.zh: 上古穆拉帕山有巨蝠，日沒即掠瓦勞人而出，夜夜擄人食之，族滅在即。醫師禳之無效。一老嫗自請犧牲：夜立村央，懷藏火棒；為蝠巨爪所攫，升空時揭棒——光芒如日之曳尾（即彗星），示人其巢之向。翌晨山巢烈焰騰空，眾尋至而誅之。至今山上有白骨巨堆。

sensitivity.note: Makusi tradition recorded by Schomburgk, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A long, long while ago an immense Bat lived on the mountain and spread fear and terror among the Makusis. As soon as the Sun had sunk in the west, the huge creature left its unknown dwelling, swept down upon the happy homes, and, swift as an arrow, pounced upon and carried off anyone whom it found out of doors: it carried the individual in its powerful claws up to its unknown nest and there devoured him. Not a night passed without an abduction, the tribe daily numbered less, and its entire annihilation seemed at hand. The medicine-man exorcised the Spirit; it returned again: the men went to discover the residence of the cursed murderer, but they did not find it — Makunaima was not with them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §203A (from Schomburgk); not verbatim.

passages.text: To prevent the total destruction of her tribe an old woman arose and declared herself ready to sacrifice herself for the good of her nation. When night fell she stationed herself, with a covered fire-stick, in the middle of the village while the remainder of the people crouched in terror within their houses. The fluttering of the wings is heard, and the heroine, seized in the creature's frightful claws, is carried aloft to the charnel house. She now uncovers the fire-stick, which — like the Sun throwing its rays backward, the Comet — shows by the streak of light thus produced the direction that the people must follow to find the mortuary house of their brethren. The high flames of fire from the burning nest upon this very mountain showed the folk next morning where to go: they succeeded in killing the creature. History does not say whether the old woman lost her life in this heroic deed; but even now immense heaps of bleached bones are to be found there.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §203A (from Schomburgk); not verbatim.

title.en: Okona-kura: the Morning Star Left in the Hole
title.zh: 奧科納庫拉：留在穴中之晨星

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §204

summary.en: The Warraus on the Pomeroon call the Morning Star Okona-kura. She it was who stuck in the hole when her people first came down from above the skies to populate the earth — the stout woman who closed the way home forever. The Makusis speak of the Evening Star as Kai-wono, wife of the Moon, because she is to be seen in his near neighborhood and shines more brightly than all the other stars. The Indians of the Casiquiare believed that the dew which falls by night was the spittle of the stars; the Caribs ascribed it to the urination of the stars.
summary.zh: 波默龍瓦勞人稱晨星曰奧科納庫拉。族人初自天下降而殖地時，即彼卡於穴中——絕其歸路之肥婦也。馬庫希人謂昏星為月之妻凱沃諾，以恆近月而光勝群星。卡西基亞雷土人謂夜露乃星之唾；加勒比人謂乃星之溺。

sensitivity.note: Guiana oral tradition summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically. Cross-reference to the Warau sky-descent record.

passages.text: The Warraus here on the Pomeroon call the Morning Star Okona-kura. She it was who stuck in the hole when her people first came down from above the skies to populate the earth. The Makusis speak of the Evening Star as Kai-wono, wife of the Moon, because she is to be seen in his near neighborhood, and also on account of her shining more brightly than all the other stars.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §204; not verbatim.

passages.text: According to Father Gili, the Indians of the Casiquiare believed that the dew which falls by night was the spittle of the stars, a belief similar to that reported of the Makusis. The Caribs ascribed it to the urination of the stars.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §204; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun and Moon Fight: Shouting at an Eclipse

region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

texts.period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1883-1915 (im Thurn, Brett, Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §§195-196

summary.en: On one occasion, during an eclipse of the sun, the Arawak men rushed from their houses with loud shouts and yells: a fight was going on between the Sun and the Moon, and they shouted to frighten and so part the combatants. Brett speaks of Oroan, the great Demon of Darkness, who causes eclipses: he seizes the Sun and strives to quench the fire, till scorched and blackened he retires, only to return another time. In Cayenne, eclipses upset the Indians a good deal: they think some frightful monster has come to devour the heavenly bodies, make a terrible noise, and shoot a volley of arrows into the air to chase it away — a total or short eclipse they consider a fatal thing.
summary.zh: 日蝕之時，阿拉瓦克男子自屋奔出，大呼大叫：日月方鬥也，呼以駭之使分。布雷特言黑暗大魔奧羅安致蝕：捉日而欲滅其火，灼黑而退，異日復來。卡宴土人謂怪獸欲吞日月，故大噪而向空發箭以逐之；全蝕或短蝕，皆視為凶。

sensitivity.note: Guiana oral tradition summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: It is said by im Thurn that on one occasion, during an eclipse of the sun, the Arawak men among whom he happened to be rushed from their houses with loud shouts and yells: they explained that a fight was going on between the Sun and the Moon, and they shouted to frighten and so part the combatants. Brett speaks of Oroan, the great Demon of Darkness, who causes eclipses: he seizes the Sun and strives to quench the fire, till scorched and blackened, he retires, only to return another time.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §196; not verbatim.

passages.text: In Cayenne, eclipses of the Sun and Moon upset the Indians a good deal: they think some frightful monster has come to devour these heavenly bodies. If the eclipse is total or of short duration, they consider it a fatal thing for them: they make a terrible noise, and shoot a volley of arrows into the air to chase away the monster.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §196; not verbatim.

title.en: Making the Moon a Field: Eclipse Rites on the Orinoco
title.zh: 為月墾田：奧里諾科蝕儀

region.en: Orinoco River (Lokeca, Saliva, Guayana, Otomac tribes)
region.zh: 奧里諾科河洛凱卡-薩利瓦-瓜亞納-奧托馬諸族

texts.period: Orinoco tribal rites recorded by Gumilla; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §201

summary.en: At an eclipse of the moon the Lokeca and Atabeca Indians believed it was about to die, and that all exposed fires would be extinguished if it did: their women, crying and yelling, seized glowing embers and hid them in the sand. The Salivas had other views: all the warriors stood in rows facing the Moon, offering their prowess, while the old men thrashed the young men with whips and the women bewailed the Moon's projected departure — their promises to fight in his favor allay his fears. As soon as the Guayanas recognized an eclipse, they took up their field implements, cut and dug, loudly proclaiming that the Moon had good reason for forsaking them since they had never made a field for him: they begged him not to go, now providing him a field to plant maize, cassava, and plantains — and there is no more working on the field in the Moon's behalf until the next eclipse!
summary.zh: 月蝕之際，洛凱卡-阿塔貝卡人以為月將死，露天之火將熄；婦人大哭，各取赤炭藏於沙中。薩利瓦戰士列隊向月，許以武勇；老者鞭笞青年，婦人泣別——戰士之許諾安其心，月遂不去。瓜亞納人見蝕即荷農具墾地，高聲曰：『吾儕未嘗為月墾田，月之去宜也；今為墾之，種玉蜀黍、木薯、香蕉，請勿去！』——蝕過即止，下次月蝕再為之。

sensitivity.note: Orinoco tribal rites recorded by Gumilla, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Some of these nations believed that it [the moon] was about to die: others that it was angry with them, and that it would give them no more light. The Lokeca and Atabeca Indians held to the death theory and were under the conviction that if the Moon were indeed to die, all exposed fires would be extinguished. Their women, crying and yelling — an outburst in which the men joined — accordingly would each seize a glowing ember and hide it, either in the sand or underground. Moved by their tears and entreaties, the Moon however recovers, and the hidden fires are extinguished: but were he indeed to die, the concealed embers would remain alight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §201 (from Gumilla); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as the Guayanas recognize an eclipse of the moon, they take up the implements used in cultivating their fields. With much talk and gesticulation, some cut the undergrowth, others clear it, and others again dig up the ground, all of them loudly proclaiming that the Moon has cause for being annoyed, and particularly good reason for forsaking them, considering that they had never made a field for him. They accordingly beg him not to go, because they are now providing him with a field, in which they propose planting maize, cassava, and plantains. With these promises and entreaties they continue at their task so long as the eclipse lasts; and, as soon as it is over, they return to their houses overjoyed — but there is no more working on the field in the Moon's behalf until the next eclipse takes place!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §201 (from Gumilla); not verbatim.
